records.name: Cuba
records.summary:
Cuba is workable for trans visitors — one of Latin America's most legally transformed countries. The 2019 Constitution bans discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity; the 2022 Family Code (66.87% referendum approval) overhauled family law; and trans people can change legal gender — the July 2025 civil-registry reform further eliminated bureaucratic hurdles for name changes. CENESEX, the state sex-education centre, runs an official trans-care programme, and Havana has a visible, state-tolerated trans community.

The counterweights are systemic rather than trans-specific: Cuba is a one-party state with no independent civil society, arbitrary-detention powers are broad, the economic crisis has degraded healthcare (hormone availability is unreliable), and police discretion is wide. There is no documented pattern of police targeting trans people as trans — the historical UMAP camps era is long past and officially repudiated — but there is also no independent recourse if something goes wrong.

For a visitor: no legal exposure for gender expression or documents; low street-hostility in tourist areas; the risk is the general absence of rule-of-law recourse.

sources.claim: LegalClarity overview (May 2026): Cuba's transformation from one of the most repressive systems (UMAP forced-labour camps for gay men, 1965-68, with 'curing' experiments) to one of the most progressive legal frameworks - the 2019 Constitution bans SOGI discrimination, the 2022 Family Code legalised same-sex marriage and adoption, and trans people can change legal gender without surgery - but a meaningful gap remains between law and daily reality.

Americas Quarterly (Sept 2022): Cuba's Family Code referendum (legalising same-sex marriage and adoption) sparked deep public debate amid record emigration and another crackdown on dissent; community discussions showed both support and resistance.

Links International Journal of Socialist Renewal (Dec 2011): 'Rainbow Cuba: the sexual revolution within the revolution' - a sympathetic first-person account challenging the claim that Cuba is homophobic; includes a timeline from the 1939 anti-gay Social Defence Code through the UMAP camps (1965-68), the 1975 Supreme Court overturning of employment limits, the Family Code (1976), and CENESEX's work.
Washington Blade (Dec 2013): Cuban lawmakers ban employment discrimination against gay workers.
Washington Blade (May 2018): Cuban authorities say they are not 'directly' targeting the partner of an LGBTI asylum seeker.

freshness.fact: Post-2022 Family Code status holds: same-sex marriage, adoption and gender-identity protections in force; the older employment-discrimination ban (2013 source) was overtaken but in a positive direction.

records.name: Curaçao
records.summary:
Also an autonomous constituent country of the same kingdom, the island's audited record is one of official intent colliding with friction: representatives of all kingdom governments agreed in 2015 on an equal-rights package for Caribbean-country LGBT residents — yet the same reporting documents Pride permit difficulties as recently as 2013 and organised parliamentary opposition that the island's own government publicly opposed while supporting the community.

Travel-culture surveys place the island inside the region's quiet tolerant mainstream. For a visitor the composite reads as low legal risk with thin infrastructure: no documented state hostility, an active but negotiating community in the capital, and no evidenced local gender-recognition pathway or care capacity. The record is brief; what exists shows institutions contested rather than hostile.

sources.claim: GlobalGayz report (2017): 'Gay Life in a Tolerant Society in Aruba' - describes the ABC islands (Aruba, Bonaire, Curaçao) as quiet nests of gay-friendliness within the Kingdom of the Netherlands, tolerant and mostly open.

Caribisch Netwerk (April 2015, in Dutch): 'Quickly gay rights in all parts of the Kingdom' - representatives of all Kingdom governments agreed LGBT people on Aruba, Curaçao and Sint Maarten should quickly get equal rights; a wishes package was presented in The Hague; documents Curaçao's Gay Pride permit difficulties (2013) and the Curaçaoan government's stated support despite parliamentary opposition.

records.name: Cayman Islands
records.summary:
Cayman law never held the criminalisation its earlier profile asserted: same-sex intimacy was decriminalised in 2001 through an Order in Council imposed from London after the local legislature refused, albeit with an unequal age of consent surviving the reform. In 2020 the Court of Appeal held that a same-sex couple's overseas marriage must be recognised, and in July 2021 roughly 600 people — including the premier, the governor and other ministers — joined the islands' first Pride parade, one of the broadest official turnouts a community there has seen.

The sharp turn came in 2022: a statute confining family status to heterosexual marriage took effect and, in March of that year, the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council rejected the challenge to it. Same-sex couples therefore have no marriage or civil-partnership status, the country that administers defence and foreign affairs declined to force the issue, and equality advocates have operated mainly through immigration and recognition rulings rather than family law itself.

sources.claim: Same article as above (canonical URL): UK MPs' criticism of the Cayman draft constitution's exclusion of gay rights.

Cayman News Service (July 2021): around 600 people, including the premier, governor, ministers and MLAs, joined the Cayman Islands' first Pride Parade, organised by the Cayman LGBTQ Foundation - a historic milestone with official support; participants were asked to refrain from excessive displays of affection.
Washington Blade (Dec 2020): 'Cayman Islands recognizes same-sex couple's overseas marriage' — the Court of Appeal rules the couple's foreign marriage is recognised.

records.name: Cyprus
records.summary:
Cyprus is workable for trans visitors. The legal framework is mid-transition: public incitement to hatred based on gender identity is a criminal offence (2015), and gender identity is an aggravating factor in hate crime (2017). A legal gender recognition bill (self-determination basis) was approved by the Council of Ministers in September 2022 and is pending in parliament; until it passes, LGR requires surgery under the 2002 Civil Registry Law — a resident-facing gap.

No traveler-facing restrictions: no bathroom law, no border issues (EU member), tourist infrastructure is Western-standard and accustomed to diverse visitors. Gender identity is not yet an explicit ground in the non-discrimination framework, and the divided island matters: the northern part (de facto Turkish-controlled) has its own LGR regime requiring surgical proof, weaker protections, and less documentation — travelers should treat the north as closer to Turkey's risk profile.

sources.claim: UPR advocacy sheet for Cyprus's 4th cycle (2024) on the situation of LGBTI persons: assesses implementation of cycle-3 recommendations. Notes progress: Law 87(I)/2015 criminalises public incitement to violence or hatred based on sexual orientation or gender identity; Law 31(I)/2017 adds prejudice motivation as an aggravating factor. Outstanding: gender identity not yet a prohibited discrimination ground in equal-treatment legislation, no action plan against homophobia/transphobia, and pending legislation on transgender persons.

European Commission Network of Legal Experts country report on gender equality in Cyprus (2024, reporting period 2023): how EU equality rules are transposed into Cypriot national law, including gender-identity-related aspects of the legal framework.

Queer Cyprus Association presentation for Cyprus's UPR: lists prior recommendations (anti-discrimination, hate-speech criminalisation, victim support, enactment of transgender-persons legislation) and developments, including the 2015 Criminal Code amendment covering SOGI incitement.

Queer Cyprus Association booklet on legal gender recognition (Diversity of Colours project, EU-funded): describes the association's solidarity line (7 days/week, confidential psychosocial, legal and social support for LGBTI+ people on identity, education, work, family, shelter, health, military service), psychologist and legal-expert networks, and LGR issues - covering both the Republic of Cyprus and the north.

ILGA report on SOGIESC recommendations at the 32nd UPR Working Group session (Jan-Feb 2019): includes the Cyprus chapter - summarises SOGIESC remarks, advanced questions and recommendations for Cyprus among 14 states reviewed.

European Commission legal experts' country report on non-discrimination in Cyprus (2020, reporting period 2019): transposition and implementation of the EU equality directives, including SOGI grounds in Cypriot law.

PinkNews (Oct 2013): Cyprus amended its penal code to criminalise incitement to violence or hatred based on sexual orientation or gender identity (up to 3 years' imprisonment or €5,000 fine); workplace protections for LGBT people added in 2004.

freshness.fact: Decriminalised 1998, civil unions since 2015, conversion therapy since banned; the 2013 penal-code source remains accurate as background.

records.name: Czechia
records.summary:
Czechia is broadly workable with an improving trajectory and a major welcoming tourist hub (Prague), offset by unprepared detention systems and elevated baseline social hostility. Legal gender recognition no longer requires surgery — the Constitutional Court struck that requirement in 2024 and the Health Ministry implemented reform in 2025 — but it still requires a medical diagnosis and 6–12 months' observation (improving, not self-ID).

If detained, the system is unprepared: the Supreme Court in November 2025 demanded prison rules for trans people, and there is a documented case of police mishandling the extradition-detention of an HIV-positive trans foreigner. About half of LGBTIQ people report being targeted by insults, assault or threats over five years, and the far-right SPD uses "deviant" rhetoric; Prague and larger cities are welcoming, but harassment is more likely in rural areas or late at night.

Bathrooms are unrestricted, there is no criminalisation of trans identity, and the Schengen border poses no trans-specific friction.

sources.claim: Czech Constitutional Court judgment PL. US 52/23 (24 April 2024), legal summary: the Court struck down the requirement that surgery including sterilisation be a condition for official legal sex change - a landmark ruling ending compulsory sterilisation for legal gender recognition in Czechia.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying Reuters report (June 2025) covers Czechia dropping the surgery requirement for legal gender change.

Ceska-justice.cz (March 2023, in Czech): administrative courts clashed over how immigration police handle detained trans foreigners - the Supreme Administrative Court (Judge Baxa panel) criticised the Prague Municipal Court's 'sarcastic moral lectures' toward an HIV-positive trans detainee in transition, and ruled authorities must properly assess whether detainees are 'potentially vulnerable persons' before placement in detention facilities.

Ceska-justice.cz (Nov 2025, in Czech): Czech prisons are unprepared for trans people and lack clear rules; the Supreme Court demands the prison concept explicitly address the needs of people in or after transition, citing the Constitutional Court ruling that no longer conditions legal gender change on surgery; the human-rights commissioner supports a binding regulation while the ministry claims existing frameworks suffice.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024 (covering 2023) chapter on Czechia: politicians' anti-LGBT speech rose from 43% (2018) to 71% (2023); 43% of LGBT+ people reported discrimination/harassment in five years, highest among trans and non-binary respondents; a drag story-time event was disrupted in Brno; the new Asylum Law includes SOGI grounds; Pride Business Forum published a trans-inclusive workplace toolkit.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (covering 2024) chapter on Czechia: after the Constitutional Court repealed the surgery requirement for legal gender recognition, the Justice Minister made transphobic statements ('to prevent men from giving birth'); the SPD party circulated anti-LGBT election leaflets; the government approved a Criminal Code amendment extending hate-crime protections to sexual orientation and gender identity (pending in Parliament).
UK Foreign travel advice for Czechia: safety and security section (terrorism threat, crime, etc.). General travel advice, not trans-specific.

Travel portal (Feb 2026): Prague and larger cities are generally welcoming for LGBTQ+ solo travellers, but harassment can occur and risk is higher in rural areas or late-night settings; practical safety tips and local resources.

OSCE/ODIHR 2024 Hate Crime Report for the Czech Republic: regularly reports data; 94 hate crimes recorded by police in 2024, 46 prosecuted, 42 sentenced; Action Plans on Combating Extremism and Prejudicial Hatred introduced 2023; ODIHR notes recording does not sufficiently distinguish hate crimes.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (timeout); the underlying ECHR document (hudoc 001-243567) relates to a Court of Human Rights judgment concerning Czechia.

Deník/ČTK (June 2018, in Czech): the Czech government supported a bill allowing same-sex marriage (46 MPs from six parties), which would replace registered partnerships; the Jsme fér ('We Are Fair') campaign welcomed the decision - context of the marriage-equality debate.

freshness.fact: Surgery/sterilisation requirement for legal gender change was invalidated per the cited 2024 Constitutional Court judgment; ILGA 2025 review and the cited court documents remain current.

evidence.title: LGBTQ rights in the Czech Republic

records.name: Germany
records.summary:
Germany is very safe for transgender visitors, with two real caveats worth knowing. First, far-right street hostility is the most documented concern: roughly 110 of 245 Christopher Street Day (Pride) events in 2025 were disrupted or attacked, over half linked to organised far-right networks — a visitor at Pride, or visibly trans in the eastern Länder, faces elevated harassment. Second, if you are arrested, prison placement follows your self-chosen civil-registry gender entry under recent state-level reforms (better than France, which still places by legal gender/ID and has subjected trans women to gynaecological "verification"), but exceptions allow placement contrary to your self-declared gender and are invoked inconsistently — a neo-Nazi provocateur who self-ID'd to female was reassigned from a women's to a men's prison in 2026 after public outcry.

Offsetting this: bathrooms are unrestricted (venue-level sauna debates only), no border-police humiliation of trans travellers is documented, and carrying personal HRT through the Schengen area is uneventful. The Self-Determination Act (self-ID) is a positive climate signal though not itself a traveller-outing factor.

Calibration note (Aug 2026): Germany recorded a ~35% rise in "gender diversity" hate-crime assaults in 2024 (1,152 cases) and a trans DJ filed an Equal Treatment Act complaint over degrading security screening at Frankfurt Airport — a real airport-outing incident, though resolved through a functioning legal complaint mechanism. sources.claim: NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying France24 piece (July 2026) covers the German neo-Nazi (legally female under the Self-Determination Act) being sent to a men's prison.

Verfassungsblog essay (March 2026, in German) 'Selbstbestimmung hinter Gittern' by Clara Wellhäußer: argues against a discriminatory special regime for trans people in prison following the Liebich controversy and the Self-Determination Act - constitutional analysis of trans incarceration.

DW (Aug 2023): how German prisons deal with trans inmates - climate activist Penelope Frank (legal sex 'male', identifies as a woman) faced being sent to a men's prison; the prison staff union says men's prisons are inadequately prepared and understaffed to protect trans prisoners; highlights the structural problem of binary-biological placement.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2026 (covering 2025) chapter on Germany: record 84,172 politically motivated crimes (mostly far-right), with 1,765 offences targeting sexual orientation (+17.75%) and 1,152 targeting gender identity; the new Merz coalition moved to end humanitarian admission programmes including for LGBTI Afghans; Education Minister banned gender-inclusive language in her ministry (contrary to anti-discrimination advice); proposal to classify Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia as 'safe countries of origin' despite imprisonment and torture of LGBTI people there.

BBC (Aug 2025): controversy over far-right extremist Marla-Svenja Liebich, who changed legal gender to female under Germany's new Self-Determination Act (simple registry declaration) after a conviction for neo-Nazi incitement; media questioned whether the change was 'serious'; the case fuelled debate over the self-ID law.

DW (July 2026): Liebich, legally registered as a woman, was transferred to a men's prison after extradition from the Czech Republic - authorities cited the safety of prisoners at the women's facility; critics called the gender change a provocation and abuse of the self-determination law.

Resident Advisor (June 2025): trans DJ BASHKKA filed a legal complaint against Frankfurt Airport under Germany's Equal Treatment Act after a male security officer questioned her gender during screening, refused her request for a female officer for a pat-down ('I don't care what you identify as. You're not a woman'), and laughed with colleagues - a documented airport-screening discrimination incident.

STOP the HATE (German campaign): information platform on hate crime against LGBTIQ* people - definitions, reporting, evidence preservation, support services, and cooperation with police and civil-society organisations.
RTL (in German): controversy over a guidance document on who may enter women's saunas under the Self-Determination Act - media debate about trans women in gendered facilities.
Tagesspiegel Queerspiegel (in German): how Berlin saunas and similar facilities are handling trans women under the Self-Determination Act - facility-by-facility practices and legal uncertainty.

Criminological Research Institute of Lower Saxony (KFN) research project 'Transgender people in prison': the German penal system relies on binary-biological separation; accommodation per gender identity occurs only exceptionally; the project studies the tension between the constitutional right to gender identity and presumed risks, noting a lack of data on numbers, experiences and needs of trans prisoners.
Berlin prison service official page (in German): information for trans, inter and non-binary persons in custody - rules and contacts across Berlin facilities.

freshness.fact: Germany's rights level (ranked among Europe's highest) unchanged; sole cited source is the ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2026 (Feb 2026), by definition current.

records.name: Djibouti
records.summary: Djibouti is dangerous for trans visitors. The penal code does not explicitly criminalise same-sex conduct, but vague “good morals” provisions (Arts 353/354) make homosexuality “de facto illegal” in practice; no anti-discrimination law, no LGR, no community infrastructure; authoritarian state with US/French bases but no rights space.

sources.claim: Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): Djibouti's penal code does not explicitly criminalise LGBTIQ identities or consensual same-sex conduct, but Sections 353-354 refer vaguely to 'good morals'; homosexuality is regarded as de facto illegal. No anti-discrimination law; the 2023 US State Department report found pervasive social and religious intolerance and fear of assembly; no LGBTIQ organisations identified.

Wikipedia overview: legality of same-sex activity is ambiguous (no law explicitly criminalising it, but 'obscene acts' provisions); limited protection based on sexual orientation; no gender-identity recognition; LGBTQ people face stigmatisation.

US State Department 2023 Human Rights Report for Djibouti: official assessment including the SOGI section - pervasive social and religious intolerance, LGBTIQ persons afraid to assemble or express themselves, no known prosecutions.

US State Department 2015 Human Rights Report for Djibouti: general human-rights assessment (suppression of opposition, harsh prisons, FGM, trafficking) - baseline context with limited LGBT-specific content.

Canadian IRB Response to Information Request DJI104070.E (2012): treatment of sexual minorities in Djibouti (2009-March 2012) - information scarce; societal norms did not allow public discussion of homosexuality; GlobalGayz reports gay people 'living undercover and in fear' with 'virtually zero tolerance'; but no known reports of societal violence or discrimination; legislation ambiguous (some sources say illegal, ILGA says not criminalised).

freshness.fact: Still no explicit homosexuality offence but 'obscene acts'/public morality provisions are used against LGBTQ people; the 2007-era framing survives in current law.

records.name: Dominica
records.summary: Dominica demands real caution. High Court decriminalised same-sex relations in April 2024 (fourth Eastern Caribbean state); the old law had allowed forced psychiatric commitment. No LGR; small community; no documented anti-trans violence pattern.

sources.claim: Human Rights Watch (Apr 2024): 'Dominica High Court Decriminalizes Same-Sex Conduct' — the Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court strikes down 'buggery' and 'indecency' provisions as discriminatory.

BBC (April 2024): Dominica's High Court overturned the ban on consensual same-sex relations - sections 14 and 16 of the Sexual Offences Act were unconstitutional, breaching liberty, expression and privacy rights. The claimant said the laws had condemned him 'to live in constant fear of criminal sanction'; activists hailed 'a significant milestone' for the Caribbean.
NOTE: This is a State Department press statement page (archived, navigation only at fetch time); the underlying statement relates to Dominica.
NOTE: This US Mission Geneva page is a generic LGBT-rights landing page (site navigation only at fetch time); no Dominica-specific content was retrievable.

Dominica News Online (July 2019): a challenge to Dominica's buggery laws was filed in the High Court by a gay man claiming the law violates numerous constitutional rights; represented by Cara Shillingford with support from Minority Rights Dominica (MiRiDom), the Canadian HIV/AIDS Legal Network, University of Toronto's IHRP and Lawyers Without Borders; Maurice Tomlinson announced the case.

Erasing 76 Crimes (May 2013): Dominica's Catholic bishop Gabriel Malzaire called for eliminating criminal penalties for homosexuality and ending 'all forms of violence' against LGBT people, citing the Holy See's UN position; the law provides up to 10 years; notes two men on a gay cruise were arrested in March 2012 for sex on board their ship (released after pleading guilty to indecent exposure).
